reviewer: u1-existing-B — independent solve-then-compare pass, blind to reviewer A

flags.detail: The key (A) is right and the core claim that an ofstream opened with ios::ate alone still truncates is correct — verified on g++ 13.3/libstdc++: writing "X" to ofstream(f, ios::ate) over a 10-byte file leaves a 1-byte file. But the rule the explanation states to justify it is over-broad and is contradicted by its own preceding clause. It says 'opening for output without ios::in is itself what discards the contents', which would make ofstream(f, ios::app) truncate — and the same sentence has just correctly said 'ios::app never discards anything'. The omitted term is ios::app: the openmode-to-stdio-mode table maps out -> "w" and out|trunc -> "w" (truncating) but out|app -> "a" and app -> "a" (not truncating), and ate is masked out of that mapping entirely and only triggers a seek-to-end after the file is opened. Likewise the claim that 'ios::ate preserves the contents only when the file is also opened for input' is false for out|app|ate, which I verified preserves ([HELLOWORLDX]). Fix: replace the rule with 'opening for output with neither ios::in nor ios::app is what discards the contents; ios::ate is masked out of that decision and only seeks to the end afterwards.'
flags.suggested: Keep key A. Reword the last sentence of exp to: "Option B inverts the risk: ios::app never discards anything, whereas ios::ate does not protect the file at all -- it is masked out of the truncation decision and only seeks to the end after opening, so an ofstream opened with ios::ate alone still truncates. What actually preserves the contents is opening with ios::in (as on an fstream) or with ios::app; opening for output with neither is what discards them."

notes: Strong batch — I agreed with the key on all 12 on an independent solve, and empirically confirmed the ones that turn on exact library behaviour (CBA destruction order; seekg(-20, ios::cur) landing at 30 and ifstream genuinely having no seekp; eofbit+failbit both set on a failed extraction, with an eofbit-only stream still testing true so failbit is indeed the bit that matters; the base handler winning on order with only a -Wexceptions warning, not ill-formedness; at(9) throwing while s[s.size()] is the well-defined null case option B was fishing for). The one flag is explanation-level, not key-level. Closest thing to a second finding I considered and rejected: in GEN-TECH2-U1-b5ce17, private inheritance is a legitimate 'implemented-in-terms-of' relationship and so option C is not purely absurd, but the option specifies private *virtual* inheritance, which has no purpose outside a diamond, and the stem gives no reason (protected access, virtual override) to prefer it over composition — so B remains the only defensible answer.
